source: seed (original case written for this app)
title: Pharma CDMO: acquire an API manufacturer?
opening: Our client is a mid-sized Indian contract development and manufacturing organisation (a CDMO) with about ₹2,400 crore in revenue. It has been offered the chance to acquire Vizag-based Andhra Fine Chem, an active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) manufacturer, for about ₹1,800 crore. The CEO wants to know whether they should do the deal.
client_context: The client makes formulations and advanced intermediates for global pharma companies under contract. About 30% of its key starting materials and intermediates are imported from China. The target is family-owned; the family wants to exit within 6 months.
objective: Recommend whether to acquire the target, and on what terms.

clarifications.answer: Two reasons: supply security (a 2023 China supply disruption stopped two of the client's product lines for 7 weeks), and customers increasingly want 'China+1' suppliers for APIs.
The client can fund the deal with cash and debt; net debt/EBITDA would rise to about 2.5x, which the board accepts.
There is one other interested bidder, a PE fund. Binding bids are due in 8 weeks.

data.label: Valuation benchmark
data.content: Listed Indian API peers trade at 13-15x EV/EBITDA; recent private API deals were done at 11-13x.
data.release_when: Candidate asks how the price compares, or about multiples/valuation.

data.label: Synergy estimates (management)
data.content: Procurement/backward-integration savings ~₹40 cr a year from year 1; cross-selling APIs to the client's customers could add ~₹25 cr EBITDA by year 3. One-off integration cost ~₹60 cr.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about synergies or what the combined entity gains.

data.label: Regulatory diligence
data.content: The target's main plant received a USFDA Form 483 with 6 observations in 2024. The response has been filed, but a re-inspection is pending. Plants that receive a warning letter typically lose US-market sales for 18-24 months.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about risks, regulatory status, quality, or due diligence.

data.label: Customer contracts
data.content: The largest customer's supply contract expires in 14 months. It has a change-of-control clause allowing termination if ownership changes.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about customer concentration risk or contract terms.

exhibits.title: Andhra Fine Chem: financial summary (₹ crore)
rows: Share of revenue from largest customer
Share of revenue from US market
exhibits.release_when: Candidate asks about the target's financials, performance or customers.
takeaways: The asking price is ~12x EBITDA (₹1,800 / ₹150 cr), in line with private deals and below listed peers.
Customer concentration is high and rising (60% from one customer).
42% of revenue is US-exposed, which matters given the pending USFDA re-inspection.

quant.question: Is the price fair on a standalone basis?
quant.solution: ₹1,800 / ₹150 cr = 12x EBITDA, within 11-13x private deals and below 13-15x listed peers.
quant.answer: 12x: fair to slightly attractive on standalone numbers

quant.question: Value of synergies
quant.solution: Run-rate synergies ~₹65 cr EBITDA (40 + 25). At ~10x, that's ~₹650 cr of value, minus ~₹60 cr integration cost → ~₹590 cr.

quant.question: Downside if the largest customer leaves or the USFDA outcome is bad
quant.solution: Losing the largest customer (60% of revenue) could remove more than half of EBITDA. A warning letter could take out much of the 42% US revenue for ~2 years. In either case, standalone value could fall well below ₹1,800 cr.
quant.answer: Value could fall by 40-60%, wiping out the synergy value

analytical_paths: Strategic rationale → standalone value → synergies → risks/diligence → price and deal structure → recommendation.
Hypothesis: 'strategically sound and fairly priced, but risks sit in customer concentration and regulatory status' → test each.
key_insights: Strategically sound (supply security, China+1) and fairly priced at ~12x with ~₹600 cr of synergies.
Two deal-breaking risks: a pending USFDA re-inspection (42% US revenue) and a change-of-control clause on a customer that is 60% of revenue.
The answer is a structured 'yes, if': protect against those risks through price and terms.
reference_solution: Rationale is strong (supply security after the 2023 disruption, China+1 demand). Standalone price ~12x EBITDA is fair; synergies add ~₹600 cr of value. But the target has concentrated customer risk (60%, change-of-control clause, contract expiry in 14 months) and regulatory risk (Form 483, re-inspection pending). Recommend proceeding only with protections: an earn-out or escrow tied to USFDA clearance and to the key customer's consent/renewal, pre-signing engagement with that customer, and a walk-away price if they won't accept it.
alternative_approaches: Build or partner instead of buy: a greenfield API plant (3-4 years) or long-term supply contracts with Indian API makers. A candidate who compares these options is showing strong judgment.
A valuation-first approach (DCF of standalone + synergies - risks) is valid if it reaches the risk-adjusted terms.
recommendation: Bid, but conditionally. Offer ~₹1,500-1,600 cr upfront with an earn-out of ~₹200-300 cr payable on USFDA clearance and renewal of the largest customer's contract. Make customer consent a condition precedent, and do focused quality diligence before binding bids. Walk away if the family won't accept risk-sharing, and pursue long-term supply agreements with Indian API makers as plan B. Risks: losing the deal to the PE bidder, and integration of a family-run culture.
interviewer_notes: Candidates who say 'yes, synergies' without diligence risks should be probed on what could go wrong.
Good candidates translate risks into deal terms.
common_pitfalls: Recommending yes or no without terms.
learning_objective: Evaluate an acquisition beyond price and synergies: find the deal-breaking risks and turn them into deal terms.

title: PE fund: invest in a diagnostics chain?
opening: A private equity fund is considering buying a 60% stake in PathCare, a diagnostics chain with 45 labs and about 600 collection centres across South India. The fund would hold it for about five years. Should they invest?
client_context: PathCare revenue ~₹500 cr, EBITDA ~₹110 cr (22%). The asking valuation is ₹2,750 cr enterprise value (25x EBITDA). The fund targets ~20% IRR (about 2.5x money in 5 years).
objective: Decide whether the investment can meet the fund's return target and what the key diligence questions are.

clarifications.answer: The fund needs roughly 2.5x its money over 5 years (~20% IRR).
The likely exit is an IPO or a sale to a strategic buyer. Listed diagnostics peers trade at 20-30x EBITDA; the fund's base case assumes an exit at ~20x.
Indian diagnostics is growing ~12% a year. It is fragmented, with pressure on routine-test pricing from online aggregators.

data.label: Management plan
data.content: Management projects revenue growing 18% a year and EBITDA margin expanding from 22% to 26% over five years.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about growth projections or the business plan.

data.label: Test-mix economics
data.content: Routine tests are 65% of volume and 40% of revenue, at ~12% EBITDA margin. Specialised tests (genetics, oncology) are 35% of volume and 60% of revenue, at ~30% margin, and growing 25% a year.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about revenue mix, test portfolio, or where margins come from.

exhibits.title: PathCare routine-test price per test vs aggregator price (₹)
exhibits.release_when: Candidate asks about pricing pressure, competition or routine test economics.
takeaways: PathCare's routine-test price is falling ~6% a year toward aggregator levels; the premium has shrunk from 40% to 31%.
Routine-test margins will be squeezed, so the margin-expansion story depends on specialised tests.

quant.question: Return under management's plan
quant.solution: EBITDA year 5 = 500 × 1.18^5 × 26% ≈ 500 × 2.29 × 0.26 ≈ ₹297 cr. Exit at 20x → EV ≈ ₹5,950 cr. Entry EV ₹2,750 cr → ~2.2x (ignoring debt and cash). Below the 2.5x target even under management's plan.
quant.answer: ~2.2x: short of 2.5x even on management's numbers

quant.question: What is needed to hit 2.5x?
quant.solution: Need exit EV ≈ ₹6,875 cr → at 20x, EBITDA ≈ ₹344 cr; or entry price ≈ ₹2,380 cr (~21.6x) for the management plan to deliver 2.5x.
quant.answer: EBITDA ~₹345 cr by year 5, or an entry EV ≈ ₹2,400 cr

analytical_paths: Returns math first (entry, growth, margin, exit multiple) → identify which assumptions matter → test them with the mix and pricing data → decide.
Market → company → deal: the attractiveness of diagnostics, PathCare's position, then valuation and returns.
key_insights: At 25x entry and 20x exit, even management's aggressive plan returns ~2.2x, below the 2.5x target; multiple compression kills returns.
Routine-test pricing is eroding toward aggregator prices, so margin expansion rests entirely on specialised tests.
The deal works only at a lower entry price (~₹2,400 cr) or with high confidence in the specialised-test growth story.
reference_solution: Compute returns: management case gives ~₹297 cr EBITDA in year 5, exit ~₹5,950 cr at 20x, ~2.2x on ₹2,750 cr. Pressure-test: routine prices falling ~6% a year toward aggregator levels, so the plan's margin expansion depends on specialised-test growth (25% a year, 30% margin). Recommendation: don't pay 25x. Bid around ₹2,300-2,400 cr, or structure with ratchets; diligence specialised-test pipeline, referral relationships and pricing.
alternative_approaches: Market-attractiveness-led approach that ends with the returns math.
Proposing a value-creation plan (shift mix to specialised, B2B hospital contracts, bolt-on acquisitions) that could justify a higher price, if it is quantified.
recommendation: Do not invest at ₹2,750 cr. The returns miss the target even on management's plan, and routine-test pricing is eroding. Re-bid at ~₹2,300-2,400 cr, or use a structure (ratchet/earn-out) linked to specialised-test growth. Make diligence priorities the specialised-test pipeline, doctor referrals and B2B contracts. Next steps: build a downside case with 4% routine price erosion and a 18x exit.
interviewer_notes: Push for the returns calculation early; many candidates talk about market attractiveness for too long.
After the exhibit, ask what it means for the margin assumption.
learning_objective: Use returns math to structure an investment decision and pressure-test the assumptions that drive it.

title: Specialty chemicals: pricing a structural adhesive for EV batteries
opening: Our client, an Indian specialty chemicals company, has developed a structural adhesive used in assembling electric-vehicle battery packs. It can replace the bolts and rivets used today. Their production cost is about ₹600 per kg. How should they price it?
client_context: Targets Indian EV and battery-pack makers (two-wheeler and four-wheeler). A German imported adhesive is used by a few OEMs; most OEMs still use mechanical fasteners.
objective: Recommend a pricing approach and a price point for the launch.

clarifications.answer: Two groups: a few OEMs already using an imported adhesive, and the majority who still use mechanical fasteners (bolts/rivets).
Win share quickly in the first two years while keeping a healthy margin; they have capacity for about 2,000 tonnes a year.
Performance is comparable to the German product in qualification tests.

data.label: Usage per pack
data.content: About 1.5 kg of adhesive per battery pack (four-wheeler equivalent).
data.release_when: Candidate asks about usage per pack/unit or tries to value it per pack.

data.label: Value versus fasteners (per pack)
data.content: Replacing fasteners saves: fastener hardware ₹1,400; 12 minutes of assembly labour at ₹600/hour; ~0.8 kg of weight, which OEMs value at about ₹200 per kg saved. Switching needs dispensing equipment of ~₹2 cr per line; a line makes ~50,000 packs a year and equipment lasts 5 years.
data.release_when: Candidate asks what the adhesive is worth to customers or what it replaces/saves.

data.label: Imported competitor
data.content: The German adhesive sells at about ₹1,300 per kg landed in India, with 8-10 week lead times and currency risk.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about competitors or alternatives.

data.label: Cost-plus norm
data.content: The company normally prices at cost plus 50% (i.e. ~₹900/kg).
data.release_when: Candidate asks how the company usually prices, or proposes cost-plus.

quant.question: Economic value to a fastener user, per kg
quant.solution: Per pack: fasteners ₹1,400 + labour 0.2 hr × ₹600 = ₹120 + weight 0.8 × ₹200 = ₹160 → ₹1,680. Less equipment ₹2 cr / (5 × 50,000) = ₹80 → net ~₹1,600 per pack ÷ 1.5 kg ≈ ₹1,067 per kg.

quant.question: Price ceiling for imported-adhesive users
quant.solution: Next best alternative is ₹1,300/kg with lead-time and FX risk, so the ceiling is ~₹1,300/kg (arguably a bit more for supply security).

analytical_paths: Cost-based floor (₹600) → competitor reference (₹1,300) → customer value (₹1,067 for switchers) → segment pricing between floor and value, leaving customers enough surplus to switch.
Value-based pricing with economic value to customer (EVC) = reference value + differentiation value, by segment.
key_insights: Cost-plus (₹900) leaves a lot of money on the table with imported-adhesive users, whose alternative costs ₹1,300.
For fastener users the value is only ~₹1,067/kg, so pricing near ₹1,300 would stop them switching; they need a lower, share-the-value price.
Two segments with different reference values call for differentiated pricing (tiers, volume contracts, bundled equipment).
reference_solution: Floor is cost (₹600/kg). Segment by next-best alternative. Imported-adhesive users: ceiling ₹1,300, so price ~₹1,100-1,200 (a discount for local supply is still a clear win for the customer). Fastener switchers: value ~₹1,067/kg, so price ~₹850-950 to leave 15-20% of value as an incentive to switch, perhaps with dispensing equipment financed or bundled. Both are well above cost. Implement through volume-tiered contracts and application-specific grades rather than list-price discrimination.
alternative_approaches: A single price around ₹1,000/kg as a simpler launch strategy, with volume discounts, is defensible if the candidate explains the trade-off.
Penetration pricing to lock in OEM qualifications (long switching cycles) is valid if margins are checked.
recommendation: Use value-based, segmented pricing: ~₹1,150/kg for OEMs switching from the imported adhesive (still ~12% below import, plus local supply); ~₹900/kg with equipment-financing support for OEMs switching from fasteners, where value is ~₹1,067/kg. Both give 50-90% gross margin over ₹600 cost. Lock in multi-year supply contracts during qualification. Risks: price leakage between segments, the German supplier cutting price, and slow OEM qualification.
interviewer_notes: Candidates often stop at cost-plus; probe with 'what is it worth to the customer?' only via hints.
common_pitfalls: Pricing at the value ceiling, leaving no reason to switch.
Not converting per-pack value to per-kg.
learning_objective: Price from customer value and the next-best alternative, by segment, rather than cost-plus.

title: Regional OTT platform: introducing an ad-supported tier
opening: Our client is a Tamil-language streaming platform with about 20 lakh paying subscribers at ₹99 a month. It is thinking of launching a cheaper ₹49 plan with ads. Should it?
client_context: Strong original content. Pays for content on multi-year deals, so costs are mostly fixed. Monthly churn is high among price-sensitive users.
objective: Decide whether a ₹49 ad-supported tier increases profit.

clarifications.answer: Increase total monthly profit within a year.
Content costs are fixed; streaming and payment costs are about ₹10 per subscriber per month for any plan.

data.label: Research on uptake
data.content: Surveys suggest the ₹49 tier would attract ~12 lakh new subscribers, but ~5 lakh of the existing ₹99 subscribers would downgrade.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about expected uptake, cannibalisation or demand.

data.label: Ad revenue
data.content: Advertisers would pay about ₹25 per ad-tier subscriber per month at scale.

quant.question: Change in monthly profit
quant.solution: Ad-tier contribution per sub = 49 + 25 - 10 = ₹64 vs ₹99 - 10 = ₹89 for premium. Downgraders: 5 lakh × (64 - 89) = -₹1.25 cr. New: 12 lakh × ₹64 = +₹7.68 cr. Net ≈ +₹6.4 cr a month.

analytical_paths: Contribution per subscriber by tier → new subs gained vs cannibalised → net profit → risks (ad fill, brand, churn).
key_insights: Cannibalisation costs ₹25 contribution per downgrader, but new subscribers more than compensate: net ≈ +₹6.4 cr/month.
The decision is sensitive to ad revenue per user and the ratio of new to cannibalised subscribers.
reference_solution: Contribution: premium ₹89, ad tier ₹64. Net effect: +12 lakh × 64 - 5 lakh × 25 ≈ +₹6.4 cr/month. Launch, but manage cannibalisation (hold back some originals for premium, cap ad load) and verify ad revenue assumptions.
alternative_approaches: Break-even framing: how many new subscribers per downgrader are needed (25/64 ≈ 0.4).
recommendation: Launch the ₹49 ad tier: it adds ≈₹6.4 cr/month. Protect premium with early access to originals, and test ad revenue in one region first. The break-even is only ~0.4 new subscribers per downgrader, so there's a margin of safety. Risks: ad-market softness and user experience.
interviewer_notes: Quick quantitative case. Always ask 'so what?' after the number.
learning_objective: Net out cannibalisation against new demand in a tiered-pricing decision.
